\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints that provide formal guarantees during autoregressive generation:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar context-free grammar) guaranteeing JSON structural validity and entity/relation vocabulary membership (virtually eliminating entity type and relation vocabulary violations); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} guaranteeing per-triple domain/range type compliance via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
The two layers compose via bitwise AND on logit masks, with the grammar layer as an enabling prerequisite.
%
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations: 15.37\% on SciERC (7 relations) and 18.46\% on DocRED (96 relations), comparable rates governed by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology scale.
\textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR by 42--99\% across three model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) with no significant F1 cost.
For the primary model (Qwen3-8B): SciERC $+$0.13\,pp ($p{=}0.58$), DocRED $+$0.50\,pp ($p{<}0.001$); other models show comparable or larger gains (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1, mistral_docred
For calibrated models, residual DR correlates with the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate, suggesting that constraint effectiveness is predictable from schema and model characteristics.
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, DR reaches $\leq$\,0.09\% (SciERC) and 0.20\% (DocRED) with relation F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming near-lossless composability.
With beam search ($k{=}4$), the full stack (LoRA + OntoCoDec + beam) achieves zero constraint violations across all four categories while preserving extraction quality (relation F1 change ${<}$0.5\,pp).
The framework generalizes to event extraction (WikiEvents: 56 event types, 80 roles) without architectural modification and eliminates event-vocabulary and role-vocabulary violations ($\to$ 0\%); where unconstrained outputs are severely off-schema, format compliance additionally enables entity extraction (Entity F1: 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%).
Per-relation independent enforcement introduces a cross-field consistency (CF) vs.\ DR trade-off: CF violations arise (up to 12\% in zero-shot) as the cost of per-slot domain/range guarantees; fine-tuning resolves this tension (CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%).
\end{abstract}

1	% Section 3 — Method (Draft)
2	% OntoCoDec: Type-Valid Information Extraction
3	% via Compiled Ontology Constraints
4	
5	\section{Method}
6	\label{sec:method}
7	
8	We present OntoCoDec, a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles ontology schemas into token-level masks enforced during autoregressive generation.
9	Unlike type-constrained code generation, IE presents three distinct challenges: (1)~entity types are inferred from free text rather than declared annotations, (2)~the entity registry is built dynamically during generation, and (3)~constraint targets are context-dependent type assignments rather than fixed grammar productions.
10	The grammar layer (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) guarantees structural validity (well-formed JSON with ontology-vocabulary membership), while the semantic layer (\S\ref{sec:semantic}) enforces domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry.
11	We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}).
12	Formal analysis of constraint composition is deferred to Section~\ref{sec:composition}.
13	
14	
15	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
16	\label{sec:formulation}
17	
18	\paragraph{IE as structured generation.}
19	Given an input text $x$, a language model generates a structured JSON output $y$:
20	%
21	\begin{equation}\label{eq:output-schema}
22	\resizebox{.88\columnwidth}{!}{$\displaystyle
23	  y = \bigl\{\texttt{entities}: [\{n_i, \tau_i\}],\; \texttt{relations}: [\{h_j, t_j, r_j, \tau^h_j, \tau^t_j\}]\bigr\}
24	$}
25	\end{equation}
26	%
27	where each entity has a name $n_i$ and type $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$, and each relation specifies head $h_j$, tail $t_j$, relation type $r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, and head/tail entity types $\tau^h_j, \tau^t_j$.
28	The output JSON Schema (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) enforces a fixed field ordering (head $\to$ tail $\to$ relation $\to$ head\_type $\to$ tail\_type) via deterministic grammar compilation.
29	This ordering ensures that the relation type $r_j$ is known before entity type fields are generated, which enables domain and range lookups in sequential masking (\S\ref{sec:dynamic-masking}).
30	
31	\paragraph{Ontology compliance.}
32	Using the ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ defined in \S\ref{sec:background}, we write $\operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau^h : \exists \tau^t,\, (\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)\}$ for domain-valid head types and $\operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h) = \{\tau^t : (\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)\}$ for the conditional range given head type $\tau^h$.
33	Our enforcement target is \emph{pair-based} type validity: $(\tau^h, \tau^t) \in \sigma(r)$ for every triple.
34	The decoder enforces this sequentially: $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ at head position, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$ at tail position. This is equivalent to the full pair check and strictly stronger than independent domain/range enforcement, because most relations have non-rectangular type signatures ($\sigma(r) \subsetneq \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$ for all 7 SciERC and 73/96 DocRED relations; see \S\ref{sec:rectangularity}).\footnote{An independent check ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) \wedge \tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r)$) would over-permit type pairs by $1.50\times$ on SciERC and $1.58\times$ on DocRED, corresponding to 33.3\% and 36.8\% spurious type pairs.}
35	Our goal is maximizing $P(y \mid x)$ subject to all triples being type-valid and $y$ being well-formed JSON conforming to Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema}.
36	
37	
38	\subsection{Grammar Layer}
39	\label{sec:grammar}
40	
41	The grammar layer compiles $\mathcal{O}$ into a context-free grammar (CFG) enforced at every decoding step via logit masking.
42	This compilation proceeds in two stages.
43	
44	\paragraph{Schema-to-grammar compilation.}
45	We generate a JSON Schema encoding the structure in Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema} with \texttt{enum} constraints restricting entity types to $\mathcal{E}$ and relation types to $\mathcal{R}$.
46	This schema is compiled into an EBNF grammar via XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, producing a pushdown automaton tracking JSON structure and enum membership.
47	
48	\paragraph{Logit masking.}
49	At step $t$, the automaton computes grammar-valid tokens $G(t) \subseteq V$; all others receive logits $-\infty$.
50	This simultaneously enforces: (i)~structural validity (well-formed JSON), (ii)~relation vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$), and (iii)~entity type membership ($\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$).
51	Domain/range constraints are \emph{not} enforced, as they depend on entity types within each triple; this gap is filled by the semantic layer.
52	
53	\paragraph{Empirical profile.}
54	On SciERC, grammar constraints eliminate relation vocabulary violations entirely (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and entity type violations entirely (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with no measurable F1 impact.
55	Domain/range violations remain effectively unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%). This confirms that grammar constraints enforce structural but not semantic validity.
56	
57	
58	\subsection{Semantic Layer}
59	\label{sec:semantic}
60	
61	The semantic layer enforces domain/range constraints through a stateful logits processor maintaining an entity registry during generation.
62	
63	\subsubsection{Entity Registry}
64	\label{sec:entity-registry}
65	
66	As the model generates the entity list, the semantic layer builds a registry $\mathcal{D}: \text{name} \to \text{type}$ mapping each entity to its declared type.
67	This registry is populated incrementally: when the model completes an entry $\{n_i, \tau_i\}$, the pair $(n_i, \tau_i)$ is added to $\mathcal{D}$.
68	The registry is then consulted during relation generation to look up the declared types of head and tail entities.
69	
70	\subsubsection{Position Detection}
71	\label{sec:position-detection}
72	
73	At each step $t$, the processor determines which field is currently being generated by pattern-matching on the decoded prefix.
74	We define five field positions (\textsc{EntityType}, \textsc{RelationType}, \textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}, and \textsc{FreeText}), identified via JSON key patterns (e.g., tokens following \texttt{"head\_type":} indicate \textsc{HeadType}).
75	Semantic masks activate only at type-bearing positions (\textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}).
76	
77	\subsubsection{Dynamic Masking}
78	\label{sec:dynamic-masking}
79	
80	At type-bearing positions, the processor computes a semantic mask $S(t) \subseteq V$ restricting generation to type-valid tokens.
81	
82	\paragraph{Head type masking.}
83	At a \textsc{HeadType} position, the processor considers the entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ and the current relation type $r_j$ (if already generated).
84	If $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only that registered type: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\mathcal{D}[h_j])\}$, ensuring consistency with both the entity list and domain constraints.
85	Otherwise, if $r_j$ is known, the mask falls back to all domain-valid types: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\tau) : \tau \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)\}$.
86	If $r_j$ is unavailable, no semantic mask is applied.
87	
88	\paragraph{Tail type masking.}
89	At a \textsc{TailType} position, the head type $\tau^h_j$ is already determined from the decoded prefix.
90	The processor computes $\operatorname{range}(r_j, \tau^h_j)$, the valid tail types conditioned on the generated head type (\S\ref{sec:formulation}).
91	If $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$, the mask further restricts to the registered type when it belongs to this set.
92	This sequential check ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) achieves exact pair-based enforcement, strictly tighter than an independent range check $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r)$.
93	
94	\paragraph{Tokenizer-agnostic type masking.}
95	Each type name $\tau \in \mathcal{E}$ must be mapped to token IDs for logit masking.
96	A naive approach maps $\tau$ to its first subword token and sets disallowed IDs to $-\infty$, but this fails in two scenarios:
97	(1)~SentencePiece tokenizers produce context-dependent tokenizations where the same string yields different token IDs depending on preceding context (e.g., after a JSON delimiter), and
98	(2)~ontologies with prefix-shared type names (e.g., \textsc{Sen}, \textsc{Sid}, \textsc{Side} in WikiEvents) map to the same first token, making single-token disambiguation impossible.
99	We resolve both with \emph{continuation masking}: at compile time, we scan the full vocabulary to build a prefix map identifying, for each type name, all tokens whose decoded text is a valid prefix.
100	At decode time, the semantic mask allows any token that continues a partially-generated type name, disambiguating over multiple steps.
101	This is tokenizer-agnostic, handling byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral) without tokenizer-specific logic.
102	
103	\subsubsection{Grammar-Semantic Interaction}
104	\label{sec:interaction}
105	
106	The final mask is the conjunction of $G(t)$ and $S(t)$, permitting only tokens satisfying both layers (formalized in \S\ref{sec:composition}).
107	This embodies an \emph{enabling dependency}: semantic lookup requires relation types to be valid members of $\mathcal{R}$, guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
108	Without grammar enforcement, the model may generate out-of-vocabulary relation types for which no $\sigma(r)$ rules exist.
109	Empirically, semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) while failing to eliminate vocabulary violations; the full combination achieves 94\% DR reduction.
110	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (the semantic layer would mask out all grammar-valid tokens), the system falls back to grammar-only control, preserving structural validity at the cost of a potential type violation.
111	This \emph{grammar-first invariant} reflects a deliberate priority ordering: structural integrity is a hard constraint, while type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation.
112	
113	
114	\subsection{Decoding Strategies}
115	\label{sec:strategies}
116	
117	\paragraph{S1: Single-pass decoding.}
118	Both constraint layers are active throughout a single generation pass.
119	The entity registry is populated as entities are generated and immediately available for relation-level type checking.
120	This is the simpler and recommended strategy. It achieves strong constraint enforcement with higher relation F1 than the two-pass alternative.
121	
122	\paragraph{S2: Two-pass decoding.}\label{sec:s2}
123	The first pass generates only entities under grammar constraints; the extracted entities compile an input-dependent grammar that additionally constrains head and tail names to match declared entities.
124	The second pass generates relations under this tighter grammar plus semantic constraints.
125	Detailed comparison is provided in the appendix.
126

1	% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)
2	
3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
12	
13	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
15	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
16	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
17	
18	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
19	We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
20	%
21	\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
22	  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
23	\end{equation}
24	%
25	where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
26	The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
27	Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
28	This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: for calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%; including Mistral (whose high baseline ET shifts the regime), the full range across all three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; quantitative analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
29	
30	\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
31	\label{sec:rectangularity}
32	% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
33	Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
34	Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{E}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: for calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%; including Mistral (whose high baseline ET shifts the regime), the full range across all three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; quantitative analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking ($\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$, then $\tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r, \tau^h)$) is necessary because real ontology type signatures are non-rectangular: 0/7 SciERC and only 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$.
Independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious type pairs; on SciERC, 100\% of residual DR under S1 are pairs that pass independent checks but violate $\sigma(r)$.

\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
We classify constraints by when sufficient information becomes available: \emph{local} (current token only, e.g., vocabulary membership; grammar layer), \emph{prefix-decidable} (decoded prefix, e.g., domain/range; semantic layer), and \emph{non-local} (forward coreference; outside single-pass decoding, partially addressed by S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).

The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.

This confirms that the three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Wall-clock overhead is modest; \texttt{early\_stopping} terminates generation once all beams produce a complete sequence, limiting the additional compute to partial-sequence exploration rather than full-length replication.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

9	\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
10	CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
11	(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
12	The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
13	(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.
14	
15	These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
16	Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
17	Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
18	This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
19	The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.

24	\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
25	\label{app:fallback-coverage}
26	The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
27	\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (36.6\% of type-bearing positions on SciERC) occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations. These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
28	\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
29	Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.
30	
31	We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
32	On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
33	On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
34	The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
35	DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
36	This metric directly quantifies the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
37	Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).

\section{Extended Discussion}\label{app:discussion}

%%% CF Dual Mechanism %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1

\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.

These mechanisms have sharply different model profiles.
Qwen3-8B triggers zero grammar-first fallbacks across all experiments, attributing 100\% of its CF violations to registry override.
Llama-3.1-8B, by contrast, triggers 5{,}882 fallbacks on SciERC (10.7 per document) and 57{,}825 on DocRED (63.8 per document), making grammar-first fallback the dominant CF source.
This asymmetry is consistent with the cross-model CF gap: Qwen achieves CF\,=\,2.57\% on DocRED vs.\ Llama's 12.02\%, despite both using identical constraint configurations.
The difference traces to Llama's less calibrated type predictions, which more frequently conflict with the semantic mask's valid set, triggering fallback.

%%% Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage %%%
% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (final data)

\paragraph{Fallback Behavior and Effective Coverage.}
\label{app:fallback-coverage}
The two-layer architecture produces two distinct fallback mechanisms with different semantic consequences.
\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (36.6\% of type-bearing positions on SciERC) occurs when $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$: the semantic layer deactivates as a safety valve, preserving structural validity at the cost of potential type violations. These events account for the residual DR that persists after constraint enforcement.
\emph{Registry-consistent fallback} (4.5\%) occurs when the entity's registered type conflicts with domain/range constraints; the system defaults to the registered type for cross-triple consistency.
Together, these mechanisms produce the characteristic profile of composable constraint systems: residual DR traces to grammar-first fallback events, while CF violations arise from registry override events where per-relation enforcement assigns conflicting types.

We define \emph{effective semantic constraint coverage} as $1 - f_{\text{gf}}$, where $f_{\text{gf}}$ is the grammar-first fallback rate.
On SciERC, Llama-3.1-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 36.6\%$ (6{,}237 of 17{,}024 mask calls), yielding 63.4\% effective coverage.
On DocRED, by contrast, Qwen3-8B shows $f_{\text{gf}} = 0.08\%$ (46 of 54{,}859), yielding 99.9\% coverage.
The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.
DocRED types (\textsc{PER}, \textsc{ORG}, \textsc{LOC}, \textsc{TIME}, \textsc{NUM}, \textsc{MISC}) are all single-token, eliminating this inflation.
This metric directly quantifies the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): it measures the fraction of decoding steps where both constraint layers are jointly active, providing a fine-grained view beyond aggregate violation rates.
Qwen3-8B, with zero grammar-first fallbacks, achieves 100\% effective coverage on SciERC, consistent with its lower residual DR (0.93\% vs.\ Llama's 0.08\%).

%%% CF-DR Trade-off Analysis %%%
% exp_ids: cf_fallback_ablation_scierc (CF fallback vs full_s1 baseline)

\paragraph{CF-DR Trade-off Analysis.}
\label{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}

CF violations are the most prominent residual limitation of OntoCoDec under zero-shot decoding (9.90\% on SciERC, up to 12.02\% on Llama DocRED).
We treat this honestly: per-relation independent enforcement cannot eliminate CF without trading it against DR.
Table~\ref{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff} reports a pilot ablation in which we replace the grammar-first fallback with a CF-priority fallback that forces the entity's registered type when it conflicts with $\sigma(r)$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{DR\,(\%)} & \textbf{CF\,(\%)} & \textbf{DR+CF} & \textbf{$f_{\text{gf}}$\,(\%)} \\
\midrule
Full S1 (baseline) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 10.83 & --- \\
CF fallback        & 14.78 & 0.04 & 14.82 & 36.64 \\
\midrule
$\Delta$ & $+$13.85 & $-$9.86 & $+$3.99 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{CF-DR trade-off pilot on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, 551 documents; \texttt{w1\_cf\_fallback\_scierc\_pilot}). CF fallback eliminates CF but re-routes violations to DR, increasing total violations (DR+CF) by 3.99\,pp. $f_{\text{gf}}$: grammar-first fallback rate at type-bearing positions.}
\label{tab:cf-dr-tradeoff}
\end{table}

The CF fallback variant nearly eliminates CF (9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.04\%, $-$9.86\,pp) but at the cost of a 15.9$\times$ increase in DR (0.93\%\,$\to$\,14.78\%, $+$13.85\,pp).
% exp_id: w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004, f_gf=0.3664
This is not a net improvement: total violations (DR+CF) rise from 10.83\% to 14.82\% ($+$3.99\,pp), so the change \emph{re-routes} violations rather than reducing them.
The mechanism is mechanical: each token position with conflicting masks must commit to one violation type; when the CF fallback forces the system to emit the entity's registered type even though it lies outside $\sigma(r)$, the resulting triple satisfies cross-entity consistency but violates domain/range.
The grammar-first fallback is triggered at 36.64\% of type-bearing positions, indicating that this conflict is structural, not a tunable hyperparameter.

We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
Within this design, the current full S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.
The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are inversely associated (Spearman $\rho = -0.77$, $n{=}6$), with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}).
The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.
While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.
The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.

Two complementary paths can lower CF without re-routing it to DR.
(i)~\emph{Reduce the baseline conflict rate.} Composing OntoCoDec with LoRA fine-tuning on SciERC reduces CF by 88\% relative to the zero-shot setting (9.90\%\,$\to$\,1.18\%; Table~\ref{tab:composability}), because the fine-tuned model's per-slot type predictions agree more often with the entity registry, so the per-relation mask and the registry intersect more frequently.
% exp_id: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval: CF=0.0118
The remaining 1.18\% still traces to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity, so this path is empirically validated on one dataset and one fine-tuning method but does not generalize without further evidence.
(ii)~\emph{Replace per-relation enforcement with global entity-level type consensus during decoding.} This is outside the scope of OntoCoDec's forward-only autoregressive design and is left to future work.

%%% Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1,
%          llama_scierc_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1

\paragraph{Dual-Factor Quantitative Analysis.}
\label{app:dual-factor}

Figure~\ref{fig:dual-factor-scatter} plots residual DR against the product $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ for model$\times$dataset configurations.
For \emph{calibrated} models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B; unconstrained ET${<}$3\% on both datasets), a linear fit yields $y = 0.366x - 0.138$ with $R^2 = 0.886$ ($n{=}4$, $F(1,2) = 15.54$, $p \approx 0.058$); with only four data points (df $= 2$) and $p > 0.05$, this constitutes a descriptive characterization rather than a confirmatory statistical test.
The strong fit supports the dual-factor pattern from \S\ref{sec:composition}: residual DR is governed by the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate.
Mistral-7B (unconstrained ET${=}$7.58\% on DocRED) deviates from this pattern: its residual DR on DocRED (33.21\%) substantially exceeds the linear prediction, confirming that when model calibration is insufficient (ET${>}$5\% on either dataset), residual DR is dominated by entity misclassification rather than constraint-search failure.
This motivates a principled exclusion criterion: models with unconstrained ET${>}$5\% on either dataset fall outside the regime where the tightness$\times$RV product is the primary DR driver.
The two DocRED points (high $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) separate cleanly from the two SciERC points (low $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), and within each dataset the model with higher baseline RV shows higher residual DR.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\columnwidth]{figures/dual_factor_scatter.pdf}
\caption{Residual DR vs.\ $\bar{\kappa} \times \text{RV}_{\text{baseline}}$ across four model$\times$dataset configurations.
Linear fit (calibrated models): $y = 0.366x - 0.138$, $R^2 = 0.886$; Mistral deviates due to entity misclassification.}
\label{fig:dual-factor-scatter}
\end{figure}

%%% Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact (moved from §7) %%%
% exp_ids: d012_bootstrap_ci (DocRED +0.50pp p<0.001, SciERC +0.13pp p=0.58),
%          phase0_docred_unconstrained (RV=29.66%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (RV=1.39%)

\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary relation names.
DocRED's baseline RV of 29.66\% produces 5{,}189 OOV predictions counted as false positives; eliminating them yields a significant precision gain.
SciERC's baseline RV is only 1.39\% (24 OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
Llama-3.1-8B's lower baseline RV (16.03\%) yields a smaller but directionally consistent improvement ($+$0.29\,pp vs.\ $+$0.50\,pp), confirming that F1 gain magnitude is proportional to baseline OOV rate.
% exp_ids: phase0_docred_unconstrained, phase0_scierc_unconstrained
% exp_ids: llama_docred_unconstrained (RV=16.03%), llama_docred_full_s1 (R-F1 delta=+0.29pp)

%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%),
%          phase0_scierc_unconstrained (DR=15.37%), phase2_docred_unconstrained (DR=18.46%)

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary: Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

%%% Paragraph 4: Decoding-Time vs. Post-Hoc Enforcement %%%
% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)

\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
Post-hoc filtering (generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions) yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions), reducing recall from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

%%% CF Violation Distribution %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=245), llama_scierc_full_s1 (CF=162),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2670), llama_docred_full_s1 (CF=3824)

\paragraph{Cross-Field Violation Distribution.}
\label{app:cf-distribution}

Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution} reports the complete distribution of conflicting-type pairs for SciERC full S1 (245 CF violations, all pairwise; no mention triggered $\geq$3 types).

\paragraph{Residual DR Error Analysis.}
\label{app:residual-dr-analysis}

Across all fine-tuned settings (2 models $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ full S1), only 36 domain/range violations remain.
Manual inspection reveals four root causes:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Entity type errors} (39\%): the LLM assigns an incorrect entity type (e.g., labeling a geographic entity as \textsc{LOC} when the gold standard requires \textsc{MISC}), causing the semantic mask to permit a domain/range-incompatible relation.
\item \emph{Schema coverage gaps} (33\%): the frequency-based constraint table, constructed from training-set co-occurrence statistics, does not cover long-tail type pairs that are ontologically valid but rare. These violations are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone.
\item \emph{Incorrect relation selection} (17\%): the model selects a semantically inappropriate relation whose domain/range constraints are incompatible with the correctly typed entities.
\item \emph{Direction reversal} (11\%): the model assigns the correct relation but inverts head/tail roles, placing entities in positions that violate the relation's asymmetric domain/range specification.
\end{enumerate}

Two dataset-specific patterns emerge.
Outside Llama DocRED, all residual violations (3 of 36, spanning Llama SciERC and Qwen DocRED) trace exclusively to schema coverage gaps: the model's entity typing is accurate, and the constraint system has reached its theoretical ceiling given the frequency-based constraint table.
On DocRED, Llama-3.1-8B contributes 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), with entity type errors as the dominant cause (14/33, 42\%).
This asymmetry reflects Llama's weaker fine-tuned entity typing on DocRED's larger ontology (96 relations, 7 entity types) compared to Qwen, which achieves near-zero residual.
The implication is twofold: (i)~the irreducible floor from schema gaps is small ($\sim$3 violations across 4 settings), confirming that the constraint system operates near its theoretical optimum; (ii)~residual violations from entity typing errors are addressable through stronger base models or improved entity typing modules, without modifying the constraint architecture.

\paragraph{Relation Matching Protocol.}
\label{app:fuzzy-matching}
Relation F1 evaluation uses fuzzy normalization to handle model-specific formatting variants (e.g., underscores vs.\ spaces, abbreviations).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly deployed for zero-shot information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
In a systematic study, we find violations are pervasive: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred}, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.
Relations with tight constraints exhibit far higher rates (\textsc{Compare}: 42.4\%) than loosely constrained ones (\textsc{Used-for}: 0.8\%).

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, enabling the semantic layer to look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
On SciERC, OntoCoDec reduces DR violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while remaining F1-neutral ($+$0.13\,pp).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), showing that violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and that prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Empirical validation on 3 models $\times$ 3 datasets (2 RE + 1 EE): DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC and $\downarrow$42--90\% on DocRED, with significant R-F1 gains (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$); cross-task generalization to event extraction on WikiEvents (vocabulary violations $\to$\,0\%; format compliance enables entity extraction, Entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%); composability with fine-tuning (DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost); and characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%).
